source.title: FaithfulSAE: Towards Capturing Faithful Features with Sparse Autoencoders without External Dataset Dependencies
source.authors: Seonglae Cho; Harryn Oh; Donghyun Lee; Luis Eduardo Rodrigues Vieira; Andrew Bermingham; Ziad El Sayed

record.tranche_reason: Uses SAE feature matching, probing, and fake-feature measurements to evaluate whether SAE representations of LLM activations are useful and stable; these are different measurements from the original toy-model study.
record.gate_note: The paper cites the superposition hypothesis and describes SAEs as a way to study it, but does not test toy-model superposition geometry, feature sparsity/importance transitions, or one-dimensional feature directions. Recorded results concern SAE feature stability and downstream probing. Cited claims and the figure-only faithfulness results were not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study reports seed-to-seed Shared Feature Ratios (SFR, cosine ≥0.7 after Hungarian matching) for Top-K SAEs on seven LLMs. These numbers bear directly on whether SAE features are stable units (V5), and they show stability is incomplete and depends on the training dataset and model. The probing and Fake Feature Ratio results compare the authors' FaithfulSAE against web-trained SAEs. They do not test whether LLMs contain recoverable sparse features (V4), so V4 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors argue that out-of-distribution SAE training data lowers seed stability. FaithfulSAEs have higher SFR than instruction-data SAEs on Pythia, but lower SFR than Pile/FineWeb SAEs on all five web-comparison models. They win 12 of 18 probing cases (all CoLA cases) and have lower FFR in 5 of 7 models (Pythia is the exception). Individual-feature interpretability was not assessed.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains Top-K SAEs on model-generated versus external datasets and evaluates feature matching, reconstruction, probing, and fake-feature ratios; it does not reproduce the original toy-network superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with training dataset, model family and size, and classification task; the text also reports higher SFR at layer 16 than layer 8 in the Pythia comparison.

fits_no_version.finding: SAEs trained on the model's self-generated data have a lower fraction of features firing on random-token inputs than web-trained SAEs in 5 of 7 models. Probe accuracy on SAE reconstructions also varies with the SAE training dataset (FaithfulSAE best in 12/18 cases).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE dictionary quality and downstream utility depend on the SAE training distribution, so dictionary features partly reflect dataset artifacts rather than only model-internal structure.

record.problems: The authors say they did not evaluate instruction-tuned or reasoning models, did not assess individual-feature interpretability, and that SFR may not reflect the complexity of high-dimensional feature spaces. The probing results cover selected classification tasks; full faithfulness metrics are presented as figures without tabulated numerical values in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: Table 6 includes Fineweb- and Pile-trained probing results as separate training-dataset conditions; these comparator rows were omitted to stay within the 60-row limit while retaining FaithfulSAE results and the full SFR tables. Table 7 Pile and Fineweb FFR rows were omitted for the same reason. Table 5 faithfulness results are figure-only in the supplied text and have no extractable numerical values. The paper's aggregate statement that FaithfulSAE wins 12 out of 18 probing cases is not an additional row.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, no sparsity-dependent transition, no geometry.
All: no test of capacity competition or dedicated dimensions.
All: no test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
Whether LLMs contain sparse features an SAE recovers. Probing and FFR only compare SAE training datasets.
Completeness and canonicality (e.g. across dictionary sizes). Only seed stability at one threshold (0.7) and one seed pair is tested; individual-feature interpretability is not assessed.
All: no test of 1-D vs multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Cross-dataset reconstruction fidelity (CE difference, L2, explained variance) for SAEs trained on different datasets; this shows dataset-dependence of SAE dictionaries.
Statement that layer 16 SAEs are more seed-stable than layer 8. No tabulated values; the tabulated Pythia layers are 18 and 24, so the source of this comparison is unclear.

record.verdict_notes: The relevance to the claim lies in the absolute SFR values, not the authors' dataset comparison. Even the best case, Pythia 1.4B at 0.71, leaves about 29% of features unmatched across seeds, and the largest model (LLaMA 8B) is about 0.1. The 'absent' cut is a judgement: SFR ≈0.1 is treated as absent stability, SFR 0.18–0.71 as partial. Results use one seed pair, threshold 0.7, Top-K SAEs, and one layer per model; no uncertainty is reported. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model superposition geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or whether important features get dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemanticity arises for reasons other than capacity pressure.

Does not directly identify features spread across neurons, establish their underlying sparsity or completeness, or evaluate individual-feature interpretability; probes measure classification information in SAE representations.
Tests seed-to-seed feature matching and some functional utility, but does not establish that SAE features are complete or canonical units.
Does not test whether the model's underlying superposed features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.
